features.title: Andy Warhol and the Street: The Pop Artist Who Painted with a Graffiti Writer
features.standfirst: Warhol never sprayed a wall, but he spent two years painting with Jean-Michel Basquiat, who began as the downtown graffiti writer SAMO. What the four-handed canvases borrowed from the street.
features.body:
Andy Warhol never wrote on a wall. He worked in a studio, printed his pictures through silkscreens and sold them through galleries. Yet the story of street art in New York keeps running into him, because in the early 1980s the most famous painter in the city spent two years making pictures with a young man who had started out spraying words around downtown Manhattan.

SAMO on the walls

From May 1978, Jean-Michel Basquiat and his school friend Al Diaz wrote short, deadpan phrases signed SAMO© on buildings in SoHo and the East Village, around the School of Visual Arts and on the D train (Wikipedia, SAMO). The Village Voice ran a piece on the mystery writer in December 1978. When the two fell out in early 1980, Basquiat finished the project by writing SAMO© IS DEAD across downtown (same source).

Around the same time he was selling hand-made postcards in SoHo. He is thought to have first met Warhol in 1979, when he tried to sell him some (The Art Newspaper). The real introduction came in October 1982, when the dealer Bruno Bischofberger brought him to lunch at Warhol's studio. Warhol took a Polaroid, and by Warhol's own account a painting came back within two hours, still wet (Wikipedia, Jean-Michel Basquiat).

Four hands, one canvas

The two are thought to have made about 160 works together between 1983 and 1985 (The Art Newspaper). The early pieces began with Warhol's own silkscreened images, eggs, crabs and dollar signs, which Basquiat painted over. Basquiat later put it simply: Warhol would start a painting and he would deface it (e-flux).

That is close to a description of street practice moved indoors. A printed, commercial image goes up first, and a second hand writes over it. Warhol said he thought the paintings were better when you could not tell who had done which part (same source). In our reading, that is the moment the two worlds meet: Pop art's ready-made pictures, and graffiti's habit of answering whatever is already on the wall.

A printed image goes up first, and a second hand writes over it.

A panned show and a long afterlife

The joint exhibition at the Tony Shafrazi Gallery in New York in 1985 did not go well. Critics panned it, one called Basquiat Warhol's mascot, and the friendship cooled (Wikipedia, Jean-Michel Basquiat). Warhol died in February 1987 and Basquiat in August 1988.

Keith Haring, who had known Basquiat from the School of Visual Arts scene (same source), described the collaboration as a conversation held through painting instead of words. When the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris showed more than 80 of the jointly signed canvases in 2023, it hung work by Haring and Kenny Scharf beside them (e-flux).

Why it matters on the street

From 1962 Warhol worked by taking a familiar photograph and printing it again and again through a silkscreen (MoMA). In our reading, the stencils, paste-ups and stickers that repeat one picture across a city work in much the same way. His paintings are still on the market this month. Our sister sites, Global Art Monitor and The Art World Report, follow the November 2026 results.

features.title: Konn Artiss: Art, Intervention and Public Attention
features.standfirst: Konn Artiss makes work for the moment a crowd realises something wasn’t supposed to be there. A profile of an artist whose best-known pieces start as public interventions and end up as arguments about who art is for.
features.body:
When people realise that what they’re looking at wasn’t supposed to be there, a crowd goes quiet for a second or two. Then the phones come out. Konn Artiss makes work for that second, and for what happens after it.

For Artiss, as for many artists of this generation, the gallery is one stop in an artwork’s life rather than its starting point. The work usually appears first in public, placed or staged somewhere that already means something, and it borrows the attention of people who weren’t looking for art. Exhibition, collection and auction come later, after the piece has been photographed, discussed and argued over.

Starting outside the white cube

“Street art” covers some of this. The unannounced appearance, the dependence on location and the sense of the city as co-author all come from the street. The strategy owes as much to performance and conceptual art, though. An intervention cares less about how it looks than about what changes when it turns up.

That changes where the viewer stands. You can admire a mural from across the road. An intervention makes you part of its audience whether you meant to be or not, and your reaction (the double take, the photo, the post) becomes part of how the work travels.

Venice as a stage

Venice sharpens all of this. The city is already a spectacle, and every other year it hosts the most closely watched exhibition in contemporary art, so its visitors arrive ready to look. Artiss’s Venice intervention used that readiness. The city provided the drama and the work interrupted it.

Several things make Venice suit this kind of art. Narrow sightlines and routes along the water turn any unexpected object into an event. Nearly every visitor carries a camera. During the Biennale the line between the official programme and unofficial responses to it blurs, and people go looking for the next thing to see. A work placed there gets compared with the pavilions, with the city, and with earlier artists who used Venice the same way. (We cover that history in Venice as a Stage for Contemporary Art.)

The city provided the drama. The work interrupted it.

Attention as a material

Critics of public interventions often call them stunts. The forms can look alike, so the reflex is understandable, but it misses how carefully serious artists in this field work. Artiss handles attention the way other artists handle paint, steel or light.

In practice that means planning for documentation, since most people will see the work on a screen and the photograph will outlive the object. It means thinking about timing and about who will be there, and checking that the piece reads at a glance and still holds up on a second look. It also means treating the public’s response, whether enthusiasm, confusion or irritation, as part of what the work means.

As with any art made in public, the real test comes after the attention moves on. Clever interventions tend to evaporate. The lasting ones leave an idea that people keep coming back to.

From the street to the collection

Every artist who works in public runs into the same practical problem: how does a temporary gesture become something that can be exhibited, bought and kept? Artiss treats the intervention and the collectable work as related but separate. The public piece makes the argument. Studio works, editions and documentation take it into private and institutional collections.

Collectors need to understand that separation. Value here depends on provenance and clarity: knowing exactly what an object is, how it relates to the public work, and who vouches for its authenticity. Gallery representation is one link in that chain. From Public Spectacle to Collectable Object explains how it works.

Why it matters now

Street Art Dispatch exists because this way of working has moved from the edge of contemporary culture to its centre. The artists we follow don’t choose between the street and the gallery. They build practices that move between the two, and they use public space to reach people that institutions rarely reach.

Artiss is a clear example of that shift. The work asks who decides where art can appear, and makes a good case that the people who own the walls no longer decide alone.

features.title: Mohamed L’Ghacham: Family Photographs on the Scale of a Street
features.standfirst: A muralist from Tangier, based near Barcelona, who paints other people’s old snapshots across whole walls. How the pictures are chosen, how they are painted, and five walls from Mallorca to Vienna.
features.body:
Most murals are made to be seen from across a street. Mohamed L’Ghacham’s are made from photographs that were never meant to leave a family album: a birthday cake being cut, children outside a house, neighbours at a table. He paints them across whole walls, in towns across Europe, and the private snapshot becomes something a whole street looks at.

From Tangier to Mataró

L’Ghacham was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1993 and is based in Mataró, on the coast north of Barcelona (Nuart Aberdeen). He found graffiti at school and only later turned to the classical painters (North West Walls). Among the painters he names as influences are Antonio López and Pere Llobera (Vision Art Festival).

His first murals were not commissions. He told Colossal they were painted in abandoned or demolished places, or simply on the edges of cities (Colossal, 2021).

How the pictures are made

The work is figurative and close to realism, with what festival organisers describe as Impressionist touches (Nuart Aberdeen). The source is almost always a photograph from the late twentieth century. Colossal noted that he looks for photographs with small accidents in them, because they make the scene feel real (Colossal, 2019). The colours are muted and the brushwork is loose and layered (same source).

The photographs come from the places he paints. By 2021 he was working from snapshots and home videos lent by neighbours and from city archives (Colossal, 2021). In Estarreja, Portugal, he used a 1930s photograph of the doctor Egas Moniz with his assistant Deolinda at Santa Marta Hospital in Lisbon, from Moniz’s own archive (mohamedlghacham.com).

Five walls

Casa Paquita, Can Picafort, Mallorca, 2017. Painted for the Saladina Art Fest on one of the oldest houses in the town. The image shows the owner Paquita’s children about forty years earlier, in the same spot, from a photograph she let him use (Street Art United States).

Por Angelo!, Lioni, Italy, 2018. Painted for the Biennale Angelo Garofalo (mohamedlghacham.com). The same year he painted De Fiesta with Alba Trench in Werchter, Belgium, for North West Walls (same source).

La Fondue, Crans-Montana, Switzerland, 2019. Painted for Vision Art Festival, which lists the wall at 1,500 metres (Vision Art Festival).

A birthday cake, Ostend, Belgium. A woman cutting a birthday cake. The city’s art route says he wanted to show the mother as a central figure in the family, and saw the cake as a sign of how things are divided unequally. The work can no longer be seen (The Crystal Ship). The date is to confirm.

the table is set, Vienna, 2025. Listed among Calle Libre’s 2025 walls, in the Meidling district. A family shares a meal while plants grow over the picture, which the festival describes as a fading memory and a small, reachable utopia (Calle Libre).

Private snapshots, painted for a whole street to see.

Off the wall

L’Ghacham also paints at studio scale. He showed with PDP Gallery at the Moniker Art Fair in Brooklyn in May 2018 (mohamedlghacham.com), and Colossal reported a planned solo show of his smaller paintings at PDP Gallery in the summer of 2021 (Colossal, 2021). We have found no public auction result for his work as of November 2026.

features.title: What Makes an Art Intervention Different from a Publicity Stunt?
features.standfirst: Both appear without warning, draw a crowd and spread online. Five questions for telling art made in public apart from marketing made to trend.
features.body:
On paper the two can look identical. Something appears in public without warning, a crowd gathers, photographs spread, and an artist’s or a brand’s name trends for a day. Most of us still sense that an art intervention and a publicity stunt are different things. Saying exactly how is harder.

The shared toolkit

Both rely on surprise, location and circulation. Both need an audience that didn’t plan to be one. Both are now made with the camera in mind, because an event nobody photographs barely happened. That overlap is why critics call artists’ work a stunt so often, and why brands keep borrowing street art’s language.

Five questions that separate them

  1. What’s left once it’s over? A stunt has done its job when attention peaks. An intervention should leave something behind: an idea, an argument, a different way of seeing a place.
  2. Does the site matter? Interventions usually belong to the place where they happen, and moving them drains their meaning. Stunts travel well. The same activation could run in any city with enough footfall.
  3. Who benefits? If the main result is a product launch or more followers, the answer is obvious. Art can raise an artist’s profile too, but the audience should get more out of it than it gives.
  4. Does it survive without the headlines? Look at what was actually made. If it’s still precise and still says something, it will outlast the photograph.
  5. Is the risk real? Artists working in public often take real legal, financial and reputational risks. Stunts are usually permitted, insured and engineered to be safe.

Three cases

During the 2019 Biennale, Banksy set up an unannounced stall in Venice selling paintings that together showed a huge cruise ship dwarfing the city. Police moved the stall on. It looked like a stunt, but the subject belonged to the place: what mass tourism does to the lagoon. The location carried the argument.

Maurizio Cattelan’s Comedian, a banana duct-taped to a wall at Art Basel Miami Beach in 2019, is harder to place. Part of its fame came from another artist eating it. Its subject, though, was how the art market decides what things are worth, so the spectacle was its medium. In 2024 an edition sold at Sotheby’s for $6.2 million, and the argument that followed made Cattelan’s point for him.

Christo and Jeanne-Claude sit at the other end. Wrapping the Reichstag in Berlin in 1995 took more than twenty years of negotiation, and the artists paid for it by selling their own preparatory works. It was slow and expensive, and few public artworks have drawn bigger crowds.

Ask what remains once the noise stops.

A working definition

An art intervention borrows the methods of public spectacle to say something that outlasts the spectacle. A publicity stunt is finished when the spectacle ends. The line isn’t always clean, and the best artists work along it on purpose (our profile of Konn Artiss looks at one). The five questions will usually tell you which side a work falls on.

features.title: Venice as a Stage for Contemporary Art
features.standfirst: A city built as a sequence of reveals, where the art world arrives every other year ready to look. Why Venice is the most loaded stage in public art.
features.body:
Venice has always been staged. A city built on water and laid out as a series of reveals (a bridge, a corner, a sudden campo) teaches visitors to look. That makes it one of the most powerful settings in the world for contemporary art, and one of the most loaded.

A city built for spectators

The Venice Biennale, first held in 1895, made an institution of that theatre. Every other year, national pavilions in the Giardini and the Arsenale bring the art world to one city, and collateral shows fill palazzos, churches and courtyards across the islands. For a few months almost any wall in Venice could be an exhibition space, and almost any visitor a critic.

Official and unofficial Venice

All that attention produces a second, unofficial Biennale. Artists without a pavilion or an invitation know the audience is in town and inclined to read anything unexpected as art. Some of the most discussed works of recent editions appeared on that fringe.

In 2019 Banksy set up an unannounced stall of paintings that together showed a giant cruise ship looming over the city. Around the same time, a mural of a child in a life jacket holding a pink flare appeared at the waterline of a canal-side building. Both dealt with things Venice lives with every day: mass tourism and migration. Neither had the Biennale’s permission, and both relied on its audience.

Sanctioned work has used the city just as boldly. For the 2017 Biennale, Lorenzo Quinn’s Support showed two giant hands rising from the Grand Canal to brace the façade of a historic hotel. The image of a city at risk from climate change spread well beyond the art press.

In Venice the setting always becomes part of the work.

Why interventions land here

Three things make Venice unusually receptive. The first is sightlines: without cars, people walk slowly and look closely. The second is symbolism. Venice already stands for beauty, fragility and overtourism, so any work placed there inherits a metaphor. The third is documentation, since visitors photograph an intervention from every angle within minutes.

The same things make the city hard to work in. A piece that only uses Venice as a backdrop looks thin beside the real thing. The interventions that last, including those by artists such as Konn Artiss, deal with what the city is as well as how it looks.

After the show

Venice also shows how fast public art turns into history. Murals fade in the salt air, temporary works come down, stalls get moved on. Documentation and memory survive, and increasingly so do the collectable objects these moments produce. That’s why our Intervention Archive treats Venice as a core city. A large share of the story of art made in public has happened on its water.

features.title: From Public Spectacle to Collectable Object
features.standfirst: A canvas shreds itself seconds after the hammer falls, then resells for eighteen times the price. How a public spectacle becomes something a collector can own.
features.body:
On 5 October 2018, seconds after the hammer fell on Banksy’s Girl with Balloon at Sotheby’s London, a shredder hidden in the frame started up and pulled half the canvas through. The room gasped. Within days the work had a new title, Love is in the Bin, and was on its way to becoming one of the best-known artworks of the century.

The buyer, who had agreed to pay £1,042,000, went through with the purchase. Three years later the shredded work came back to auction and sold for £18,582,000. The shredding had made the object far more valuable.

The paradox of public art

Art made in public is hard to own. A mural belongs to its wall, and an intervention happens and is gone. Even so, street and urban art has one of the busiest markets in contemporary collecting. It works by translation: the public event is carried into objects that can hold its meaning inside a collection.

What collectors actually buy

  • Studio originals. Unique works on canvas, panel or paper, made for exhibition and sale. They are often the closest link to an artist’s public practice.
  • Editions and prints. Screen prints and other multiples, usually signed and numbered. Shepard Fairey built much of his practice around editions, so for him the print is central.
  • Relics and documentation. Objects, photographs and certificates tied to a specific intervention. Their value depends entirely on clear provenance.
  • Certificates and instructions. Some works exist mainly as an idea. Cattelan’s Comedian is sold as a certificate of authenticity with instructions, and the banana itself can be replaced.

Provenance is everything

Street-based work is easy to imitate, so authentication matters more here than almost anywhere else in contemporary art. Banksy’s works are authenticated by Pest Control, the artist’s own handling service. It refuses to authenticate pieces made on the street, as a stand against people removing public works to sell them. Other artists rely on their galleries, studios and catalogues.

For a new collector the rules are simple. Buy from galleries and auction houses that can document an object’s history. Ask exactly what you’re buying: a unique work, an edition (which number, out of how many) or documentation. Be wary of anything said to have come off a wall.

The shredding made the object worth eighteen times more.

Where the value comes from

The market tends to reward the qualities that make public art matter in the first place: a clear idea, a memorable moment, a recognisable voice. An intervention that really changed the conversation gives every related object a story, and in collecting a story adds value. The best galleries in this field show street-rooted artists alongside the context of their public work.

The shredder’s lesson for collectors is that in this field the artwork and the event are now bound together. The most interesting collections take account of both.

features.title: Banksy and the Evolution of Art Interventions
features.standfirst: Bristol walls, museum hangs, a month-long residency, a theme park and a self-shredding canvas: how one artist turned the intervention from trespass into a global event.
features.body:
No artist has done more to define the modern art intervention than Banksy, and none has changed the form as often. Following the work from Bristol’s walls to the auction room shows how the intervention itself developed, from trespass into a carefully planned public event.

1990s: the wall

The early work came out of Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s. Stencils became the signature, partly because they’re quick to apply and partly because they produce images that read instantly. At this stage the intervention is simple: an image in the wrong place, saying something the wall’s owner never meant to say.

2005: the institution

In 2005 the target moved from the street to the museum. Banksy hung altered works without permission in New York institutions including the Museum of Modern Art and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and placed a fake “ancient” rock carving of a figure pushing a shopping trolley in the British Museum. Some of these stayed up for days before anyone noticed. The question underneath was who decides what counts as art.

2006–2013: the system

Next the interventions went after systems instead of places. In 2006 hundreds of copies of a Paris Hilton album in UK record shops were swapped for versions the artist had re-sleeved and remixed. In October 2013 the month-long Better Out Than In residency put a new work somewhere in New York every day, and the city became a scavenger hunt played out online. On one day a stall near Central Park sold signed canvases for $60 each, and almost nobody stopped to buy.

2015–2019: the experience

By the mid-2010s the interventions had become places you could walk into. Dismaland (2015), a dystopian “bemusement park” on a derelict lido in Weston-super-Mare, brought together dozens of artists for five weeks. The Walled Off Hotel (2017) in Bethlehem faces the separation wall and runs as both a hotel and an exhibition space. In 2018 the shredding of Girl with Balloon turned an auction room into the stage. In 2019 the Venice stall and mural took on the Biennale, and later that year Gross Domestic Product, a Croydon shop window that never opened, played out a trademark dispute in public.

The surprise stayed constant. The audience grew from one passer-by to the whole internet.

What changed

Surprise runs through all three decades. Scale and planning changed. The early stencils depended on someone happening to notice. The later interventions were built to circulate worldwide: confirmed on the artist’s own channels, documented by the studio, and set up so that the public’s reaction became part of the work.

Banksy wasn’t working alone. Invader’s tile mosaics, appearing in Paris since 1998, and Shepard Fairey’s sticker campaign, started in 1989, built their own systems for occupying the city. All three are in our Intervention Archive.

The legacy for today’s artists

Every artist working in public now, Konn Artiss included, works in a landscape Banksy helped shape. Audiences expect art to appear without warning, the press knows how to cover it, and the market knows how to price what comes out of it. The next generation has to find interventions that can still surprise an audience that has learned to expect surprise.

features.title: How Banksy’s Style Works: Girl with Balloon and Laugh Now
features.standfirst: A stencil, a single colour and a line of dry text. How Banksy builds an image that reads in a second, shown through two of his best-known pictures.
features.body:
Banksy’s pictures are built to be understood in a second. A flat black figure, one line of text or one patch of colour, and a twist that turns the image against whoever is in charge. This piece looks at how that style works, using two well-known images: Girl with Balloon and Laugh Now.

The method: the stencil

A stencil is a sheet with shapes cut out of it. Hold it to a wall, spray paint through it, and the image appears in seconds. Banksy came out of Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s, and the stencil became his signature there (Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art research guide). The guide describes him as an early mainstream innovator of stencil graffiti.

The same stencil can be used again on a wall, a canvas or a print, which is why one image can exist in many forms. On canvas he often mixes spray paint with acrylic or household emulsion. He also makes screenprint editions and sculptural pieces from found objects.

What you see in the work

“Street art” and “stencil graffiti” are the established labels. What follows is our own description of what the pictures share:

  • Hard edges. Figures are flat silhouettes with crisp outlines, with no shading or brushwork.
  • A small palette. Mostly black and white, often with a single accent colour, frequently red.
  • Familiar characters. Rats, chimpanzees, children, police officers and soldiers stand in for people and power.
  • Short, dry text. When there are words, there are few of them, and they carry the joke.
  • One idea per image. The picture reads at a glance, then the sting follows.

Girl with Balloon

The image first appeared as a stencil on London’s South Bank, near Waterloo Bridge, in 2002 (JSMA guide; Wikipedia). A small girl in black silhouette reaches towards a heart-shaped balloon drifting out of reach. The balloon is the only red in the picture, so the eye goes straight to it.

Most of the picture is empty space between the girl and the balloon, and that gap is the story. Our reading: it can be seen as loss, hope or letting go, and it is left open on purpose. The image was later made as canvases and screenprint editions. In October 2018 a framed version was partly shredded by a device hidden in its frame at Sotheby’s London moments after it sold, and was renamed Love is in the Bin (From Public Spectacle to Collectable Object).

Laugh Now

A stooping chimpanzee wears a sandwich board that reads “Laugh now, but one day we’ll be in charge”. The 2001 canvas, in acrylic and spray paint and 91.5 by 91.5 cm, was described in Bonhams’ catalogue for its October 2026 sale as a dark silhouette cut sharply against a pale green ground (Bonhams lot 9). The same note records that the motif was scaled up in 2002 as a six-metre mural commissioned by the Ocean Rooms nightclub in Brighton.

Here the street method moves onto canvas unchanged: one figure, one flat colour behind it, one line of text. Our reading: the joke flips who is on top. The figure looks submissive, but the words carry a threat.

One figure, one colour, one line. The joke lands first and the point follows.

Why it matters

The style explains much of how the work travels. An image that reads in a second works on a wall, on a phone screen and on a print. For collectors, it also means the same image can appear as a unique canvas or as an edition of hundreds, which is why it always matters to ask exactly which one you are looking at. Every authentic work is certified by Pest Control, the artist’s own authentication body.

features.title: Five Street Artists, Five Styles: From São Paulo to Yogyakarta
features.standfirst: Painted dream worlds, carved faces, X-eyed cartoons, stitched comics and quiet figures. How five street artists from five continents built styles you can recognise from across a street.
features.body:
Street art no longer has one home. The five artists here started on walls in São Paulo, Lisbon, New York, Yogyakarta and South Africa, and each built a style you can recognise from across a street. This piece looks at how each style works, through two pictures per artist.

OSGEMEOS, São Paulo

The twin brothers Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo started as graffiti artists, and their name means “the twins” in Portuguese (Artsy). Their walls and canvases share one dream world of thin, yellow-skinned figures in patterned clothes.

In 2007 the owners of Kelburn Castle in Scotland asked four Brazilian street artists, OSGEMEOS among them, to paint the outside of the 13th century building (Hyperallergic). The figures and patterns wrap round towers and turrets, treating the whole building as one surface. In the studio the same world becomes objects: Sem medo de ser feliz (2010) is acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins on panel (Christie’s). The sequins make the surface glitter, something a wall cannot do.

Vhils, Lisbon

Alexandre Farto works by taking away rather than adding. He cuts, drills, etches or blasts into walls, posters, doors and metal until a face appears (vhils.com). His Scratching the Surface walls were first shown in Lisbon in 2007 and at the Cans Festival in London in 2008 (same source).

The studio works use the same idea on smaller things. Attrition series #01 (2018) is a stack of advertising posters collected from the street and carved by hand, so the colours of old adverts become the light and shade of a face (Bonhams). In our reading, the portraits seem to come out of the city’s own layers.

KAWS, New York

Brian Donnelly tagged “KAWS” on walls in New Jersey and Manhattan, then began painting his own cartoon figures onto bus shelter adverts (Christie’s guide). The figures have X’s for eyes, and the main character, COMPANION, first appeared as a toy in 1999 (same source).

The toy grew into sculpture: COMPANION (ORIGINALFAKE) (2011) is fibreglass and paint, almost two and a half metres tall (Christie’s). The paintings crop the cartoons tight. CAMO CAN’T HELP YOU (2013) breaks its figures into flat zones of colour with crisp edges across a canvas three metres wide (Christie’s).

Eko Nugroho, Yogyakarta

Eko Nugroho makes murals, paintings, embroidery and sculpture, often with local communities (Singapore Art Museum). His figures come from comics and are usually masked; the museum says he avoids stereotyped faces on purpose (same source).

His embroidered picture Illusion (2007), now at the Singapore Art Museum, shows a stripped landscape with monster-like machines and a masked figure (same source). Trap Costum for President 1 (2011) uses the same stitched comic style for a joke about power (Christie’s). Moving a wall image into thread keeps it flat and bright.

Faith XLVII, South Africa

Faith XLVII began writing graffiti on South African streets in 1997 as Faith47, and has since painted public murals in 39 countries (Strauss & Co). Her figures are calm and almost religious, often with a Latin or Afrikaans phrase.

Her 2014 mural Capax Infiniti on the Carlyle building in Portland, Oregon, later became a lithograph with the same title (Strauss & Co). The triptych Coltan; Oil; Diamonds, mixed media on panel in frames she made by hand, names three resources mined in Africa (Strauss & Co). In our reading, the three panel altarpiece shape joins her spiritual style to a political subject.

Five cities, five methods: paint, carving, cartoons, thread and quiet figures.

What they share

Each artist kept the street’s need to be read at a glance, then found a studio form that adds something a wall cannot: sequins, carved paper, fibreglass, embroidery or a hand-made frame. Recent auction results for all five are on our sister site, Global Art Monitor.

features.title: Why Contemporary Artists Are Working Beyond Gallery Walls
features.standfirst: The white cube was designed to remove distractions, and many artists now find that neutrality limiting. Five reasons the work is moving outside.
features.body:
The white cube was designed to remove distractions: clean walls, even light, nothing between the viewer and the work. A growing number of contemporary artists now find that neutrality limiting. They’re taking work into streets, squares and waterways and onto screens, and their reasons go well beyond rebellion.

1. The audience is elsewhere

Most people never visit a contemporary gallery. Public space reaches commuters, residents, tourists and children. Keith Haring understood this in the early 1980s, when he drew in chalk on the black paper covering unused advertising panels in the New York subway and made work for thousands of riders a day.

2. Context is content

A work placed somewhere specific takes on that place’s history and politics. JR’s huge paste-ups get their meaning from where they go up, from the portraits in Women Are Heroes to the 2016 illusion that made the Louvre pyramid seem to vanish.

3. Documentation travels further than objects

A gallery show reaches the people who visit. A public work that gets photographed and shared can reach millions within hours. The image of an intervention now counts as a work in its own right, and it’s often how most people experience it.

4. Participation changes the work

Public art lets people in. JR’s Inside Out project, launched in 2011, asks communities around the world to paste up their own portraits. Invader’s Flash Invaders app turns finding the mosaics into a game played across cities. The audience takes part as well as looking.

5. The gallery still matters, differently

The gallery isn’t finished. Its role is shifting from the place where art starts to the place where it’s gathered, explained and kept. Galleries working with street-rooted artists show studio works, editions and documentation that carry a public practice into collections.

The work starts in the street. The gallery keeps the story.

The risks

Working outside the gallery has costs. Unsanctioned work can bring legal trouble, temporary work can disappear without a record, and public attention moves on quickly. Careful, searchable, accurate documentation matters for exactly that reason, and it’s why Street Art Dispatch is building an archive of public interventions.

columns.title: The Phone Is the New Plinth
columns.standfirst: Every public artwork now lives twice, once on the street and once on the screen. Most of its audience only ever sees the screen.
columns.body:
Every public artwork now has two lives, one on the street and one on the screen. For most of its audience the screen is the only one they see.

Artists working in public have adapted quickly. They compose works to read in a vertical frame, time them for when feeds are busiest, and release their own documentation so that the first image to circulate is the right one. Social platforms did for urban art what the printing press did for the poster, making the image endlessly reproducible and putting it in everyone’s pocket.

That brings opportunity and pressure. An artist with a strong online following can work without institutions. The platforms reward novelty over depth, though, and it’s tempting to make work for the scroll instead of the street.

The most interesting artists use the phone the way a sculptor uses a plinth: to present the work, which still lives somewhere else.

columns.title: Anatomy of a Viral Artwork
columns.standfirst: What makes a work of public art travel? The same four ingredients keep turning up, and quality isn’t one of them.
columns.body:
What makes a work of public art travel? Across the most-shared interventions of the past decade, the same ingredients keep turning up.

  1. A readable image. The work makes sense in under a second, even as a thumbnail.
  2. A recognisable setting. A famous building, a symbolic city or a familiar street.
  3. A story. Something happened, such as a removal, an arrest, a sale or a disappearance, that gives people a reason to share it.
  4. An open question. Who made it? Is it real? Is it allowed?

Going viral says nothing about quality, and plenty of strong work never travels. Knowing the mechanics helps audiences and editors tell work built to last from work built to trend. For the longer argument, read What Makes an Art Intervention Different from a Publicity Stunt?

columns.title: When the Crowd Becomes the Medium
columns.standfirst: Some interventions aren’t objects. They’re situations, and the public is the material.
columns.body:
Some interventions aren’t objects at all. They’re situations, and the crowd is the material.

Think of the queue outside a shop that never opens, the people gathered around a work that might be removed at any moment, or the hunt across a city for the next piece. In each case, part of the artwork is what the public does.

That puts public art close to performance, in a line that runs back to the happenings of the 1960s. It also raises a question of responsibility. When a crowd becomes the medium, the artist is shaping how people behave in public space as well as what it looks like.

The best work uses that power carefully and gives people something worth discovering.

artists.name: Konn Artiss
artists.summary: An artist working across public intervention, installation and collectable work. Our readers know Artiss best for an intervention staged in Venice that made the city’s audience part of the piece.

artists.name: Banksy
artists.summary: The anonymous artist from Bristol’s graffiti scene who made the stencil a global language and turned interventions into events, from unsanctioned museum hangs to a canvas that shredded itself at auction.
facts: Hand-cut stencils, spray paint, screenprint editions

artists.name: Invader
artists.summary: The French artist whose ceramic-tile mosaics, built from the pixel language of early video games, have been “invading” cities since 1998. In 2015 one reached the International Space Station.

artists.name: Shepard Fairey
artists.summary: The American artist who grew a 1989 student sticker campaign into the OBEY project. His 2008 Hope poster became one of the defining political images of its era.

artists.name: OSGEMEOS
artists.summary: Twin brothers from São Paulo who started as graffiti artists and built one dream world of thin, yellow-skinned figures, painted on walls, canvases and once on a Scottish castle.
facts: Spray paint, acrylic, sequins, found doors

artists.name: Vhils
artists.summary: The Lisbon artist Alexandre Farto, who makes portraits by cutting, drilling and blasting into walls, posters, doors and metal rather than adding paint.

artists.name: KAWS
artists.summary: The American artist Brian Donnelly, who began by painting cartoon figures onto bus shelter adverts and turned his X-eyed character COMPANION into toys, paintings and giant sculptures.
facts: Flat colour, cartoon figures, X-ed out eyes

artists.name: Eko Nugroho
artists.summary: The Yogyakarta artist whose masked, comic-book figures move from walls into paintings, embroidery and batik, often made with local communities.

artists.name: Faith XLVII
artists.summary: The South African artist who began writing graffiti as Faith47 in 1997 and has since painted public murals in 39 countries, with calm, almost religious figures.

artists.name: Mohamed L’Ghacham
artists.summary: A painter and muralist from Tangier, based in Mataró, who turns old family photographs into wall-sized paintings for festivals across Europe.
facts: Murals painted from late 20th century photographs

artists.name: Grove Gallery roster
artists.summary: Street Art Dispatch is expanding its profiles across the artists shown by Grove Gallery. Each one covers public work alongside studio practice, editions and collecting context.

archive.title: JR at the Louvre

Street-removed works Banksy’s Pest Control will authenticate
glossary: A unique work made by the artist for exhibition or sale: canvas, panel, paper or sculpture. It’s the closest link to a public practice.
A multiple, usually a screen print, produced in a fixed run and signed and numbered. Ask for the edition size and the number.
The documented history of ownership from the studio to you. In street art, gaps in provenance are a red flag.
Who stands behind the work: the artist’s studio, an official body such as Pest Control, or the representing gallery.
